intro: Chiang Mai's oldest named tree was planted to mark the city itself. When King Kawila resettled Chiang Mai, in a reign that ran from 1782 to 1813, a yang na went into the ground beside the Inthakin, the city pillar, in the courtyard of Wat Chedi Luang. Thailand's Ministry of Culture lists it as a heritage tree, 30 metres tall and 6 metres round. A large branch fell in April 2026 and the tree still stands, about ten minutes on foot from Tha Phae Gate.
meta_description: The yang na of Chiang Mai's city pillar at Wat Chedi Luang: planted under King Kawila, about 200 years old and 30 metres tall.
question_meta: Chiang Mai's oldest known tree is the yang na beside the city pillar at Wat Chedi Luang, put at 200 to about 230 years.
question_answer: The oldest known tree in Chiang Mai is the yang na, Dipterocarpus alatus, beside the Inthakin city pillar in the courtyard of Wat Chedi Luang. The Ministry of Culture gives its age as 200 years and Chiang Mai News put it at 226 in 2026, so somewhere between 200 and 230 is the honest figure.
question_context: The tree was planted as the city pillar's partner when King Kawila resettled Chiang Mai, in a reign that ran from 1782 to 1813, and in Thai it is called a tree that marks the city. The Ministry of Culture lists it among its Heritage Trees of the Land as Yang Na Rom Mongkhon, 30 metres tall and 6 metres round, with an age of 200 years. Chiang Mai News gave 226 years in 2026 and an older count says about 210, and none of the figures comes from counting rings. In 2021 specialists judged it at risk and a rescue project was run for it. On 16 April 2026, during the Lanna new year, a large branch broke off near the shrine of the giant Kumphan with no storm blowing and hit a power pole and a parked van. Tree surgeons from the Royal Forest Department treated the wound, and the tree stands. Wat Chedi Luang was founded in the 14th century and honours the pillar each May in the Inthakin festival. Foreign visitors are usually asked for a small ticket at the gate, and modest dress is expected.

faq.q: How old is the yang na at Wat Chedi Luang?
faq.a: About 200 years by the Ministry of Culture's register, and 226 by Chiang Mai News in 2026. Nobody has counted its rings, so read it as 200 to 230.

faq.q: Did the big tree at Wat Chedi Luang fall?
faq.a: No. A large branch broke off on 16 April 2026 and hit a power pole and a parked van. Royal Forest Department tree surgeons treated the wound and the tree still stands.

faq.q: Do you pay to enter Wat Chedi Luang?
faq.a: Foreign visitors have been asked for a small ticket at the gate; the price was not confirmed. Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered.

trees.story:
This tree was planted to mark a city. When King Kawila resettled Chiang Mai in the reign that ran from 1782 to 1813, a yang na went into the ground beside the Inthakin, the city pillar, as its partner. In Thai it is a ton mai mai mueang, a tree that marks the city.

Thailand's Ministry of Culture lists it among its Heritage Trees of the Land as Yang Na Rom Mongkhon, 30 metres tall and 6 metres round, and gives its age as 200 years. Chiang Mai News put it at 226 in 2026, and an older count says about 210. None comes from counting rings, so somewhere between 200 and 230 is the honest figure.

In 2021 specialists judged it at risk and a rescue project, Save Yang Na, care for Inthakin, was run for it. Then on 16 April 2026, around six in the evening on Pa Pi Day, the Lanna new year, a large branch snapped off near the shrine of the giant Kumphan with no storm blowing. It hit a power pole and a parked van. Tree surgeons from the Royal Forest Department treated the wound, and the tree stands.

It grows in the courtyard of Wat Chedi Luang, a temple founded in the 14th century, beside the shrine of the pillar, which is honoured each May in the Inthakin festival. The temple is about 10 minutes on foot from Tha Phae Gate. Expect a small ticket for foreign visitors at the gate.

trees.access: Wat Chedi Luang is open to visitors daily by day; foreign visitors have been asked for a small entry ticket (price not confirmed, check at the gate); modest dress (shoulders and knees covered, shoes off in halls). The tree stands in the courtyard beside the Inthakin shrine, where the pillar hall is entered through the compound.
trees.transport: In the old city: about 10 minutes on foot from Tha Phae Gate; songthaew or Grab from the station or airport.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 30 metres tall and 6 metres round. It stands in the courtyard of Wat Chedi Luang beside the shrine of the Inthakin city pillar; another yang na may stand close by.
trees.verify_notes: One of the huge yang na trees at the shrine of the Inthakin city pillar (Sao Inthakin), planted in King Kawila's time (reign 1782 to 1813) when Chiang Mai was resettled, as a tree paired to the pillar, 'tree that marks the city' (ต้นไม้หมายเมือง). Register (2017, Ministry of Culture): 'Yang Na Rom Mongkhon', age 200 years, girth 6 m (registered figure, not re-measured), height 30 m, coordinate 18.786917,98.986528. Age conflict: register 200; Chiang Mai News 17 Apr 2026 says 226 years; a 2006 tree-contest blog says about 210. All consistent with 200 to 230, none from a ring count. Alive and its state: a large branch snapped on 16 Apr 2026 around 18:00 (Pa Pi Day, the Lanna new year) near the shrine of the giant Kumphan, hit a high-voltage pole and a parked van; no storm at the time, per the temple's own security staff (Chiang Mai News). Arborists (Royal Forest Department tree-care team) treated it, and a 2021 'Save Yang Na, care for Inthakin' rescue project for the same tree had already been run after specialists found it at risk (search summaries of mgronline 2021 and Chiang Mai News 2026-04, only the latter fetched). The abbot said the break was not an omen (Komchadluek, summary). The tree is rooted in a ritual: the annual Inthakin festival (Khan Dok) in May. Pin: register point is about 60 m from an iNat GPS fix (3 m) on a Dipterocarpus at 18.78667,98.98618 and an OSM 'Landmark tree' node at 18.78654,98.98606 (historic=memorial), which agree within about 20 m, so the individual tree is placed there; the register point is the loose one. Possibly a second yang na stands nearby (a Thai summary says 'the paired yang na of the pillar'), so check which crown in the photo. Wat Chedi Luang itself dates to the 14th century. Two sources agree, alive in 2026.
